title: The questions
hook: three questions in the grave: who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man

segments.voice: Yesterday, barzakh, the grave, and your line: the in-between. Did you greet anyone across the barrier? Today, what the hadith say happens first in that in-between. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is this man who was sent among you? Three questions. No multiple choice, no notes, no time to look anything up. In the hadith that tell of the grave, these are the questions two angels ask, soon after the mourners have walked away. One hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even says the dead person hears the footsteps of the people leaving. Then the questions begin. Today, the questions, and why, in these hadith, the answers can't be crammed.
screen: `THREE QUESTIONS.` → `NO NOTES, NO LOOKING IT UP.` → `THE FOOTSTEPS WALK AWAY.`

segments.voice: The long hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, collected by Abu Dawud, lays it out. Two angels come and sit the person up. Who is your Lord? The believer says: my Lord is Allah. What is your religion? My religion is Islam. Who is this man who was sent among you? He is the Messenger of Allah. A hadith in Tirmidhi gives the two angels names, Munkar and Nakir. Then the other side of the scene. The one who lived without faith is asked the same three questions, and the answer, in paraphrase, is: I don't know. I heard people saying something, so I said it. That's the whole failure. Not a wrong theory. A borrowed answer. Something repeated without ever being one's own. The Qur'an has a verse that a hadith in Bukhari ties to this moment. In Pickthall's words: "Allah confirmeth those who believe by a firm saying in the life of the world and in the Hereafter." A firm saying. The answer holds in the grave because it was held in life. Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it. You can't memorize your way through these questions the night before, because they aren't really testing memory. They're asking what you actually lived by. Who did you turn to, when it counted? What way did you follow, on an ordinary day? Whose example did you keep? That's the point of today's line: answer now. The grave's exam is set in advance, and every day is a chance to work on the answers.
screen: `TWO ANGELS SIT THE PERSON UP.` · `MY LORD IS ALLAH.` · `I HEARD PEOPLE SAYING SOMETHING.` · then, large: `A FIRM SAYING, HELD IN LIFE.`

segments.voice: The practice: answer the questions now, in your own words. Settle, and breathe. Take the first one, slowly. Who is my Lord? Don't recite. Ask instead: who, or what, did I actually turn to this week when things went wrong? Breathe. Then the second: what way do I live by, really, when no one is watching? Breathe. Then the third: whose example am I following? If you're Muslim, you may want to say the answers the hadith gives, and then ask whether this week said them too. If you're not, let your honest answers be what they are, without judging them. The bell holds the time.
The questions. Three asked in the grave, the hadith say: who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man. Today's word.
Your line: answer now. Today, pick one of the three questions and let one small choice answer it on purpose. Tomorrow, the trumpet. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims teach the three questions of the grave to children, and at burials those present may pray for the deceased to be made firm when the angels question them.
